Landmark project · Palais Ksar Saïd, Tunis · 2016–2017

عـهـد الأمــــان

L'Éveil d'une Nation

Art at the dawn of modern Tunisia (1837–1881). An exhibition by the Rambourg Foundation with the Institut National du Patrimoine and the Ministry of Cultural Affairs.

The story

Palais de Ksar Saïd · 27 November 2016

For the first time, the Tunisian state entrusted a public collection and a public building to a private organisation to restore and exhibit them. The Palais Ksar Saïd, closed since 1956, opened its doors to the public for the first time.

01 — The palace

Ksar Saïd, the seat of power before the protectorate

A few hundred metres from the Bardo Museum, the Palais Ksar Saïd witnessed the great reforms of the 19th century and the life of the last Husainid beys. The Treaty of Bardo, which placed Tunisia under French protection in 1881, was signed in one of its rooms.

Left abandoned after independence, the palace was cleared, restored and opened to visitors for the very first time.

02 — The reforms

The beys who set Tunisia on the road to modernity

The story begins with Ahmad Bey, the first reformer, who abolished slavery in 1846. In 1857 the Ahd al-Aman — the Fundamental Pact — guaranteed the safety of people and their property, whatever their religion, and in 1861 Tunisia adopted its first constitution.

A whole chapter of pre-colonial history, long left out of the national story, was told again through paintings, manuscripts, furniture, jewellery, medals and documents.

03 — The documents

The Dostour of 1861

Alongside the Ahd al-Aman, the exhibition showed the Constitution of 1861 — the texts on which the modern Tunisian state was gradually built, and the foundation of its civil and religious courts.

04 — The restoration

300 works brought back to life

Paintings and furniture from the collection held at Ksar Saïd were restored in seven months — a record for a project that would usually take two or three years. The Institut National du Patrimoine lent works from its collection, and the Rambourg Foundation funded the great majority of the project.
